To trace these metrics back prior to Agrippa and the Golden Dawn, one must look to the primary manuscript traditions of practical Kabbalah, medieval grimoires, and ancient textual variants. Each of the metrics used in the Wheel of the Shem ha-Mephorash has deeper, often conflicting historical roots:

1. The 72-Name Derivation (Exodus 14:19–21 Variants)

The Metric Used: The Masoretic text (vowel-stripped Hebrew consonants) combined with the boustrophedon (alternating left-to-right and right-to-left) method.

Older / Alternative Sources:

The Septuagint (LXX, c. 3rd–2nd Century BCE): The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible. If the 72 names were derived using the Greek Septuagint text rather than the Hebrew Masoretic text, the letter counts and consonant sequences would diverge entirely, as the Greek text handles grammatical constructs, spelling, and verse flow differently.

The Samaritan Pentateuch: An independent textual tradition of the first five books of Moses diverging from the Masoretic text in thousands of places. Using the Samaritan consonantal text for Exodus 14 would yield a completely different set of 72 triplets.

The Dead Sea Scrolls (4QExodᵃ or 4QExodᵇ): Fragmentary Hebrew texts of Exodus dating from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE. Some manuscript variants show slight orthographic differences (extra or missing matres lectionis like vav or yod), which would alter the exact consonant positions in the 216-letter matrix.

2. Tribal Correspondences and Camp Layouts

The Metric Used: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa’s De Occulta Philosophia (Book III, 16th century), which synthesized Renaissance Christian Cabalah.

Older / Alternative Sources:

The Book of Numbers (Chapters 2 and 10): The foundational biblical text describing the camp arrangement of the tribes around the Tabernacle (Judah, Reuben, Ephraim, Dan on the four quarters). However, Numbers does not explicitly map the tribes to astrological decans or zodiac signs—that was a later hermetic layer added centuries later.

Midrash Rabbah (Numbers Rabbah, c. 5th–12th centuries): Early rabbinic commentaries detailing the banners (degalim) and colors of the tribes, which predate Agrippa's esoteric mapping and often differ in how specific tribal attributes are characterized.

The Testament of Solomon (c. 1st–3rd Century CE): An early pseudepigraphal text featuring Solomonic command over demons and astrological decans, though it organizes angelic and demonic hierarchies differently than later Renaissance grid systems.

3. Decan Rulers (Chaldean Order)

The Metric Used: The standard Chaldean planetary order (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon) mapped across the 36 decans.

Older / Alternative Sources:

The Tetrabiblos of Claudius Ptolemy (2nd Century CE): Formally codified the planetary rulerships of the zodiac and decans in classical Greco-Roman astrology, drawing on earlier Hellenistic and Babylonian astronomical logs.

Mesotopotamian Astrological Compendia (e.g., MUL.APIN, c. 1000 BCE): The earliest surviving Babylonian star catalogs that laid out the paths of the moon and stars, which partitioned the sky into early precursors of decanal boundaries long before the Chaldean planetary hours were formalized.

4. Gematria and Letter Values

The Metric Used: Standard Hebrew letter values (Absolute / Gematria Ragil, where Aleph=1 to Tav=400).

Older / Alternative Sources:

Sefer Yetzirah (Book of Creation, c. 3rd–6th Century CE): The oldest extant Hebrew text on Jewish cosmology and letter mysticism. It assigns cosmological and elemental properties to the 22 letters (3 mothers, 7 doubles, 12 elementals) but relies less on computational word-sum balancing and more on structural permutations.

Aramaic Targumim (e.g., Targum Onkelos and Targum Jonathan, c. 1st–4th Century CE): Ancient Aramaic translations of the Hebrew Bible. In early mystical traditions, Aramaic letter values or alternative orthographies were sometimes applied before standard Hebrew square script (Ketiv Assyri) and its fixed numerical values were universally standardized across all esoteric schools.

5. Ana Bekoach and Theophoric Suffixes (-Yah / -El)

The Metric Used: The Ana Bekoach prayer (attributed to 1st-century sage Rabbi Nehemiah ben Hanina, though popularized later) and standard Golden Dawn-era suffixing (-Yah / -El).

Older / Alternative Sources:

Magical Papyri (PGM - Papyri Graecae Magicae, 2nd BCE – 5th CE): Greco-Egyptian magical texts utilizing hybrid divine names (combining Yahweh, Elohim, Greek deities, and angelic suffixes). These operational texts show that the practice of appending divine name fragments to invoke specific powers predates medieval Kabbalah by over a millennium.

1. The Textual Base: Dead Sea Scrolls & Samaritan Pentateuch

What changes: If you bypass the Masoretic text (which was standardized by the Masoretes between the 7th and 10th centuries CE) and use the older Dead Sea Scrolls (such as fragmentary Exodus scrolls from Qumran dating to the 3rd–1st centuries BCE) or the Samaritan Pentateuch, the letter counts and orthography of Exodus 14:19–21 shift.

The Result: Because ancient Hebrew orthography often lacked full vowel letters (matres lectionis like vav or yod), dropping back to Qumran-era variants would alter letter positions in the 216-letter matrix. Some of the 72 triplets would literally spell different phonetic roots, changing the divine names entirely. You would be operating on a textual foundation closer to the actual Second Temple period rather than medieval European scribal conventions.

2. The Mesopotamian Alternative: MUL.APIN and the Paths of Enlil, Anu, and Ea

What changes: As noted, Babylonian astronomy did not use abstract $10^\circ$ decan rulers. Instead, the MUL.APIN tablets (c. 1000 BCE) divide the sky horizontally into three distinct stellar paths: the Path of Enlil (northern stars), the Path of Anu (equatorial belt, $\pm 17^\circ$), and the Path of Ea (southern stars).

The Result: There are no math-driven $5^\circ$ or $10^\circ$ mathematical boxes here. "Rulers" were actual rising constellations, heliacal risings of bright stars (like the Pleiades or Sirius), and specific deities. If you apply this to a grid like the Shem ha-Mephorash wheel, you strip away the rigid geometry of the Renaissance decans and replace it with a stellar geography based on when physical constellations cross the horizon relative to the paths of the gods.

3. Linguistic Layer: Aramaic Targumim & Pre-Square Script Semitic Orthography

What changes: Using Aramaic Targumim (such as Onkelos or Jonathan) and early Semitic scripts (like Paleo-Hebrew or Phoenician script variants prior to the adoption of Aramaic square script) shifts the value and visual geometry of every letter.

The Result: In Paleo-Hebrew, letters are pictographs. An Aleph isn't just the number 1; it's an ox head. A Vav isn't just 6; it's a tent peg or hook. Translating the mechanics into early Semitic orthography means gematria stops being a purely abstract mathematical game and reverts back to visual, structural engineering where letters act as physical tools.

4. Mystical Framework: Sepher Yetzirah (The Structural Blueprint)

What changes: Long before Christian Kabbalists mapped the Tree of Life to European tarot cards, the Sepher Yetzirah (Book of Creation) laid out the cosmos using strictly the 22 Hebrew letters divided into 3 Mothers, 7 Doubles, and 12 Elementals.

The Result: The wheel isn't governed by planetary hours in the modern sense, but by the breath, the spheres, and the elemental gates. The 12 single letters map directly to the 12 elemental foundations of the universe, acting as the underlying skeleton beneath any later astrological additions.

5. Operational Execution: The Greek Magical Papyri (PGM) over Ana Bekoach

What changes: Dropping the medieval Ana Bekoach prayer in favor of the Greek Magical Papyri (PGM) shifts the operational style from structured Jewish pietistic meditation to Greco-Egyptian operative theurgy.

The Result: The PGM relies heavily on barbarous names (voces magicae), hybrid invocations (invoking Yahweh alongside Hermes, Hecate, and solar deities), and direct, coercive ritual commands. Instead of praying to an angel via a symmetrical grid, you use raw, ancient transliterated name-formulas designed to tear open the veil and compel spirits directly through sheer phonetic vibration.
